opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, it's less of a formal process than people might assume. A big part of it is just: does this defense matter? If a paper is getting a lot of attention, or people are actually deploying the idea, or it's being cited as evidence that some problem is "solved," then it's worth checking whether that's true. If nobody will ever use it, breaking it doesn't teach anyone much.

The second thing I look for is whether breaking it would teach us something general. I'm not very interested in finding a small bug in one implementation and moving on. What I want is for the attack to show a category of mistake. Maybe the defense only works because it makes gradients hard to compute. Maybe it was evaluated against an attacker who doesn't know the defense exists. Maybe the threat model quietly assumes something no real adversary would accept. If breaking one defense lets me write down "here's why this whole family of ideas doesn't work," that's far more valuable, because then the next ten papers don't have to make the same mistake.

And a lot of it, if I'm honest, is a kind of smell test. After you've done this for a while, you read a paper and certain things jump out. The robustness numbers look too good. The evaluation uses a weak attack and never tries an adaptive one. The authors say "we tried our best and couldn't break it" without showing what they tried. Those are usually the ones that fall over quickly, and sometimes the break is almost embarrassingly easy. I don't enjoy that part, because I'm not trying to dunk on anyone. But it's useful to show people what a proper evaluation looks like.

The ones I find most rewarding are the opposite case: a defense that's careful, that the authors clearly stress-tested, where I go in assuming I'll break it and I can't, or it takes me weeks. That tells you something real too. So I'd say it's a mix: impact, whether there's a general lesson, and whether my gut says the claims are stronger than the evidence.

fable-5.1.text:
That's a good question, and honestly my answer has changed a bit over time. Early on, I mostly just went after whatever was getting attention. If a paper claimed robustness and people were citing it, that was reason enough. And that turned out to be a pretty decent heuristic, because the defenses that get attention are the ones that will actually get deployed, or that will shape what other people build on top of. If a defense is wrong and nobody is paying attention to it, it doesn't really matter that it's wrong.

But the thing I've come to care about more is whether breaking it teaches us something. There's a version of this work that's basically just whack-a-mole, where you take a new defense, you run the standard attack with slightly better tuning, and it falls over, and you write it up. That's useful in a narrow sense, but after you've done it twenty times, the twenty-first one isn't telling anyone anything new. What I'm looking for now is a defense where I can't immediately see why it should fail. If I read the paper and my gut says "this is obviously broken, here's how," then it's probably not worth much of my time, because someone else will get to it or it'll just quietly not get adopted. The interesting ones are where the authors have a real argument, where there's some principle that would make it work, and I have to actually think about whether the principle holds. Those are the cases where even if I succeed, I learn why the principle fails, and that's a result that generalizes.

The other thing I'd say is that I try to pick defenses where the evaluation was done carefully but still missed something. Because that's the most important lesson for the field. If a defense was evaluated badly, breaking it just tells people "evaluate better," which everyone already knows. But if smart, careful people did a thorough evaluation and there's still a hole, then you've found a blind spot that's probably shared by a lot of other work too. That's the kind of thing I want to find.

And then practically, there's just the question of whether I think I can actually do it in a reasonable amount of time. Some things I'm pretty sure are broken but I can't see a clean path, and those I'll sometimes put down and come back to later. The ones I end up spending the most time on are the ones where I keep thinking about them when I'm not at my desk. That's probably the real answer: I work on the ones I can't stop thinking about.

astra-6.text:
I usually start with two questions: if this defense worked, would it actually be useful? And is there a reason to think it might work?

The first matters because you can make a system very secure by making it do nothing. But that’s not particularly interesting. I want to look at defenses that preserve the thing people want to use the model for, while making a clear claim about what an attacker can’t do.

Then I want to understand the idea behind the defense. Is it addressing the underlying problem, or is it just making the attacks we already know about fail? Those are very different things. If someone develops a defense against a particular set of attacks and evaluates it on that same set, there’s a good chance a slightly different attack will get through.

And I do tend to be drawn to strong defenses—things that have survived some scrutiny, or that people are seriously considering deploying. Breaking those tells us something useful about where the limits are. The goal isn’t just to get a model to say something embarrassing. It’s to figure out whether the security claim holds up when somebody actually tries to defeat it.

sol-6.1.text:
I usually start by asking: if this defense actually worked, would it matter? Would it let us do something useful that we can't safely do today? And then I ask whether there's a concrete claim I can test. What is the attacker allowed to do, what does success look like, and what is the defense supposed to prevent?

The defenses I find most interesting are the ones where the authors have made a serious effort to attack their own system and there's still something left to understand. If something fails to the first obvious attack, you can demonstrate that, but you don't necessarily learn very much. If there's a plausible reason it might work, then figuring out where that reasoning breaks can teach you something more general.

And I try to distinguish between making an attack fail and making the underlying task hard for an attacker. Those can look very similar in an experiment. A lot of the work is asking whether the defense has actually removed the vulnerability, or whether I just need to change how I'm looking for it.
